lesson.menu_title: Some People Think So, Others Do Not
lesson.menu_desc: Phase 3 -- ellipsis and substitution, for arguing without repeating yourself -- 38 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 28 -- Some People Think So, Others Do Not -- Ellipsis and Substitution
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Mark Kazuyoshi Seki Omagari | Lesson 28 -- Some People Think So, Others Do Not
lesson.grammar_point: ellipsis and substitution (so/not, do/does/did, so/neither + auxiliary, one/ones, bare to)

listenings.text: Hi Mark. Last class you learned to build the sentence that carries your opinion. What matters is. The problem is whether. I think that. Today you learn the opposite move, which is knowing what to leave out. Here is the idea. English hates repeating a phrase that both people already have in their heads, so instead of saying it again, English drops in a small word and moves on. Will the second poll change anything? I hope so. That tiny word so is standing in for a whole clause, the second poll will change something. Say I hope yes and you have said something nobody actually says. There are five of these substitutes, and every one of them is short. So and not, after think, hope, believe, guess and be afraid. Do, does and did, standing in for an entire verb phrase, as in she trains harder than I do. So plus auxiliary plus subject, for agreeing with something positive: so do I. Neither plus auxiliary plus subject, for agreeing with something negative: neither do I. And one and ones, for a noun you have already named, as in the ones who voted no. Now the trap, and it is the same trap every time. The auxiliary has to match the sentence you are answering. I am tired, so am I. I play on Saturdays, so do I. I have finished, so have I. Most students learn so do I first and then use it for everything, which is why so do I keeps coming out after I am tired. Before class, write five short answers agreeing with things your sister says, and change the auxiliary in every one of them. See you in class, Mark.

Thank you. Three people have spoken before me and all three of them said the same thing, so I am not going to say it a fourth time. I am going to say the part nobody has said yet. Everybody in this hall wants more sleep. The yes camp does, the no camp does, and so do the teachers, whatever they told you this morning. That is our common ground, it is the only piece of common ground we have, and I would like us to stop arguing about it. What we disagree about is not the morning. It is the evening. If the day starts at nine it finishes at four, and the students who lose that hour are not the ones sitting in the front row of this hall. They are the ones on the four fifteen bus, the ones with training, the ones with a job on Saturdays. Nobody in the yes camp has answered them, and I have read every comment on that poll. Then there is the part that is going to decide this whether we like it or not. An extra hour of buses costs money. I asked the office on Tuesday and nobody there could tell me how much, which tells you exactly how far this plan has got. So here is what I want. Not a second poll with the same question, because we already know the answer to that one. A second poll with the price printed at the top of the page. If this school still says yes after reading that number, I will back it. Until then I will not, and I do not think you should either. Thank you.

extra_audio.text: First, say which side you are on in one short sentence, because a listener who does not know your position cannot follow anything that comes after it. Then name the common ground, so the other side hears that you understood them before you start disagreeing with them. After that, give the single strongest reason you have, and give only that one, since a long-winded list makes the strong reason sound as weak as the last item on it. Next, ask the other side the one question they have not prepared for, because a question they cannot answer does more work than three arguments of your own. Finally, say what would change your mind, so the room hears somebody who is arguing rather than somebody who is only repeating.

reading.rtitle: Four Hundred Answers, and the School Is Still Split in Two
paras: The poll closed on Wednesday with four hundred and twelve answers, which is more than any poll this school has ever run. The question was one line long: should the school day start at nine instead of eight? Fifty-one per cent said yes, forty-three said no, and the rest did not answer at all. A result like that is not a consensus. It is a photograph of a school divided almost exactly in half, and everybody who read it found something in there to back up what they already thought.

The ones who voted yes said the same thing in different words. They are exhausted, the first lesson is wasted, and nobody learns anything before half past eight. The ones who voted no did not disagree with a word of that. They pushed back on the consequence instead. If the day starts an hour later it also ends an hour later, and the students with training, a Saturday job or a long bus journey lose that hour at the other end. Several teachers sided with them, and so did the two drivers who came to the meeting.

The debate on Friday made the split worse rather than better. The first three speakers were long-winded, and by the second one the hall had stopped listening, because every argument was redundant: it had already been made, twice, in the poll comments. Then a student from the ninth year trimmed the whole case down to four sentences. She named the only common ground anybody had found, which is that everybody in the building wants more sleep, and then asked the yes camp one question they had not prepared for. Who pays for the extra hour of buses? That single question swayed at least forty people in the room, and it was the shortest speech of the afternoon.

The head of the school has stayed neutral throughout, and she said again on Friday that she will not decide a divisive question on a fifty-one per cent vote. A second poll opens in March with the cost of the buses printed at the top of the page. Whether that changes anybody's mind is another matter. The first poll told us what the school feels. The second one will have to tell us what the school is willing to pay for.
